scenes.title: The Definition of Maxim
scenes.summary: A maxim is a general statement about matters of action; maxims are the conclusions or premises of enthymemes without the syllogism, as in Euripides' lines on educating children, and with the reason added they become enthymemes.

scenes.title: Four Kinds of Maxim
scenes.summary: Maxims come with or without a supplement: those known beforehand or clear at once need none, the paradoxical or disputed need one, and the most admired are enthymematic, like “Do not keep your anger immortal”.

scenes.title: When to Use Maxims
scenes.summary: Laconic and riddling sayings suit them, as Stesichorus told the Locrians; maxims become the old and the experienced, suit indignation and exaggeration, and even hackneyed ones are useful, like Hector's “One omen is best”.

scenes.title: Proverbs and Maxims Against the Common
scenes.summary: Some proverbs are maxims; one may speak against famous sayings like “Know yourself” and “Nothing too much” to show character or emotion, and must make one's choice clear or add the reason.

scenes.title: The Use of Maxims
scenes.summary: Maxims help because the hearers are pleased to hear their own particular opinions stated in general terms, and above all because they make speeches show character.
